results.content:
### Filler Within The Result Set

Even in US searches where the system found the subject correctly, the 80 slots were padded with material that can’t match anyone specific. On one search, the Facebook section returned a large wedding group photo, a family portrait containing several adults and children, two couple photographs and a group-of-friends shot — most carrying amber “Likely match” labels.

A group photograph of eight people isn’t a face match to an individual, and labelling it as a likely match to one isn’t informative.

### Dead Links

A meaningful share of profile links in paid reports resolved to pages that no longer exist, pointing to a stale index. For a product whose paid deliverable is clickable profile links, that’s a straightforward defect. [...] The interface is the weakest part. It doesn’t distinguish an account that probably belongs to the person from one that merely displays their face, doesn’t explain that “80 matches found” means twenty candidates per platform, and titles reports after whichever result it ranked first rather than after the image you searched. Those aren’t matching problems. They’re presentation problems, and they’re fixable.

Three changes would make this considerably more defensible: label whether a result is a likely owned account or an appearance elsewhere; carry the in-coverage labelling discipline into edge cases; and title reports after the searched image. None requires better technology. [...] The criticism is a wording one. The page headline reads “80 matches found.” Not “80 candidates,” not “showing 20 per platform.” The word matches carries a strong implication, and the number is identical on every search regardless of subject, which means it conveys nothing about what was actually found.

That’s a legitimate UX problem. A user who has paid for a report and reads “80 matches found” reasonably concludes the system found 80 things. It found a page-full of candidates, most of them unlabelled.

### Out-of-Scope Robustness Tests

None of what follows determines whether this product is accurate. These sit outside the company’s stated coverage, and I’m reporting them separately because they describe how the system behaves at its edges.

# Face2social

## Face2social

Face recognition search across public social media profile pictures.

You upload a photo. We match facial geometry — not pixels — against public profile pictures on Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and X, and return candidate profiles in about 30 seconds, from a corpus of roughly a billion images. Because the match is on the face rather than the file, it survives crops, filters and re-saves, which is exactly where classic reverse image search gives up.
